Appendix A Molecular orbital calculation details

A.1 LCAO Hückel Molecular Orbitals

The HMOs of t-stilbene are found using the same technique as in Ref. [30]. Here, the onsite energy is taken to be ℰc=−6.7​eV\mathcal{E}_{c}=-6.7\text{eV} and nearest-neighbor resonance integral given by the following [94, 95],

Hi​j=−0.63​ℏ2me​xi​j2​δi,i±1=−2.45​eV,H_{ij}=-0.63\frac{\hbar^{2}}{m_{e}x_{ij}^{2}}\delta_{i,i\pm 1}=-2.45\text{eV}, (22)

where xi​jx_{ij} is the distance between atoms. It should be noted, however, that these parameters become irrelevant after obtaining the HMOs when taking into account configurational interactions since new semi-empirical parameters are used for the single and many-body integrals as described by Pariser, Pople, and Parr [66, 67, 65].

A.2 Form Factor Details

Of the excited states beyond s1s_{1}, the s3s_{3} and s4s_{4} transitions provide the largest corrections to the scattering rate for a wide range of DM masses. In Fig. 10 we show their form factors squared in the qz=0q_{z}=0 plane. The s3s_{3} form factor has a larger amplitude, and an approximately rectangular symmetry. Compared to the s1s_{1} form factor, |fs3|2|f_{s_{3}}|^{2} extends to larger values of qxq_{x}, parallel to the long axis of the molecule. The s4s_{4} transition exhibits a rougher version of the approximate hexagonal symmetry of |fs1|2|f_{s_{1}}|^{2}, but with each peak stretched along the qyq_{y} direction, and with enhancements to the peaks at ϕ∼120∘\phi\sim 120^{\circ} and ϕ∼−60∘\phi\sim-60^{\circ}. This is because the s4s_{4} transition corresponds to one-electron excitations confined to the phenyl rings, so one should expect more spread-out support in qq-space. The localized character of the A1→H+1{}^{1}\!A\to{}^{1}\!H^{+} transition, in Platt notation, is discussed in detail by Beveridge and Jaffé (see e.g., Fig. 4 in [63]).

The relative importance of each excited state to the scattering rate is shown in the fractional modulation plot of Fig. 11. At 2​MeV2\,\,\text{MeV}, around 65%–70% of the FDM=1F_{\rm DM}=1 scattering rate occurs via the g→s1g\rightarrow s_{1} transition. Around 15%15\% of the FDM=1F_{\rm DM}=1 rate is due to the s3s_{3} transition, with s2s_{2} and s4s_{4} each contributing at the 7–8% level. For FDM=(α​me/q)2F_{\text{DM}}=(\alpha m_{e}/q)^{2} the s3s_{3} and s2s_{2} transitions have somewhat greater importance, comprising 23%23\% and 11% of the rate, respectively, compared to the 60% fraction of the rate generated by s1s_{1}. We note that the conspicuously small contribution of s2s_{2} serves as an independent confirmation of our molecular orbital model since the 1Ag1→{}^{1}A_{g}\to2Bu1{}^{1}B_{u} transition of t-stilbene in known to present an anomalously weak oscillator strength [96].

As indicated in Fig. 7 and Fig. 8, the dominance of the s1s_{1} transition is lessened at larger mχ≫10​MeVm_{\chi}\gg 10\,\,\text{MeV}, due in part to the greater kinematic accessibility of the s5s_{5} and s8s_{8} transitions, but the s1s_{1} still comprises nearly 50% of the total scattering rate, with s3s_{3} and s4s_{4} providing the leading corrections. Furthermore, is it expected that at these larger mχm_{\chi}, s5s_{5} and s8s_{8} contribute a larger portion of the overall rate since they are the lowest lying classically-allowed Bu1{}^{1}B_{u} transitions with strong oscillator strengths. Meanwhile the hierarchy of the s3s_{3} and s4s_{4} transitions comes primarily from their qq-dependent morphology since they are both Ag1{}^{1}A_{g} transitions with roughly the same Δ​E\Delta E.

Appendix B Statistics of daily modulation

Here we discuss two methods for obtaining analytic limits of Eq. (17) and Eq. (19) in the simple two-bin analysis that we utilize in this paper.

B.1 Skellam Distribution

For a two-bin example, the likelihood and test statistic can be derived directly from the Skellam distribution [97]. Given two bins (1) and (2), with mean expected numbers of events μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2}, the probability of measuring a difference Δ​N=N1−N2\Delta N=N_{1}-N_{2} between the numbers of events N1,2N_{1,2} in the two bins is given by

P⁡(Δ​N|μ1,μ2)=e−(μ1+μ2)​(μ1μ2)Δ​N/2​IΔ​N​(2​μ1​μ2),\displaystyle P\left(\Delta N|\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\right)=e^{-(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2})}\left(\frac{\mu_{1}}{\mu_{2}}\right)^{\Delta N/2}I_{\Delta N}\left(2\sqrt{\mu_{1}\mu_{2}}\right), (23)

where Ik​(z)I_{k}(z) is the kkth modified Bessel function of the first kind, and where we have assumed Poisson statistics for the distribution of events in each bin. Defining

μtot≡μ1+μ2,μΔ≡μ1−μ2\mu_{\rm tot}\equiv\mu_{1}+\mu_{2},\qquad\mu_{\Delta}\equiv\mu_{1}-\mu_{2} (24)

for convenience, the mean μ0\mu_{0}, variance σ2\sigma^{2}, skew and excess kurtosis of the Skellam distribution are [98]

μ0\displaystyle\mu_{0} =μΔ,\displaystyle=\mu_{\Delta}, σ2\displaystyle\sigma^{2} =μtot,\displaystyle=\mu_{\rm tot}, (25)
γ1\displaystyle\gamma_{1} =μΔμtot3/2,\displaystyle=\frac{\mu_{\Delta}}{\mu_{\rm tot}^{3/2}}, γ2\displaystyle\gamma_{2} =1μtot,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\mu_{\rm tot}}, (26)

so that in the large μtot\mu_{\rm tot} limit the distribution is approximately Gaussian.

An exact version of the test statistic can be derived from the double-sided distribution,

L(h)=−2​ln⁡λ(h),\displaystyle L^{(h)}=-2\ln\lambda^{(h)}, λ(h)=∑|j|≥|Δ​N|P⁡(j|μ1(h),μ2(h)),\displaystyle\lambda^{(h)}=\sum_{|j|\geq|\Delta N|}P(j|\mu_{1}^{(h)},\mu_{2}^{(h)}), (27)

where the index (h)(h) refers to the null or modulating hypotheses, (0)(0) or (m)(m). The difference between the test statistics,

Δ​L≡L(m)−L(0)=−2​ln⁡λ(m)λ(0),\displaystyle\Delta L\equiv L^{(m)}-L^{(0)}=-2\ln\frac{\lambda^{(m)}}{\lambda^{(0)}}, (28)

quantifies the significance of a signal and obeys a χ2\chi^{2} distribution with two degrees of freedom.

If μ1,2≫3\mu_{1,2}\gg 3, the Skellam distribution is well described by the Gaussian

P⁡(Δ​N|μ1,μ2)\displaystyle P(\Delta N|\mu_{1},\mu_{2}) ≃12​π​σ2​exp⁡(−(Δ​N−μΔ)22​σ2),\displaystyle\simeq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\exp\left(-\frac{(\Delta N-\mu_{\Delta})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right), (29)

with σ2=μtot\sigma^{2}=\mu_{\rm tot}, where the higher moments γ1,2\gamma_{1,2} become negligible. In this limit λ\lambda can also be approximated by an integral over a continuous variable,

1−λ\displaystyle 1-\lambda =∫μΔ−|Δ​N|μΔ+|Δ​N|d​n​P​(n|μ1,μ2)\displaystyle=\int_{\mu_{\Delta}-|\Delta N|}^{\mu_{\Delta}+|\Delta N|}\!dn\,P(n|\mu_{1},\mu_{2})
≃erf⁡(|Δ​N−μΔ|2​μtot).\displaystyle\simeq\erf\left(\frac{|\Delta N-\mu_{\Delta}|}{\sqrt{2\mu_{\rm tot}}}\right). (30)

The significance of a measured Δ​N\Delta N can be easily expressed in terms of a number of standard deviations NσN_{\sigma} by inverting the error function:

Nσ=2​erf−1⁡(1−λ)\displaystyle N_{\sigma}=\sqrt{2}\erf^{-1}\left(1-\lambda\right) ≃|Δ​N−μΔ|μtot.\displaystyle\simeq\frac{|\Delta N-\mu_{\Delta}|}{\sqrt{\mu_{\rm tot}}}. (31)

As an example, we apply this result to a modulating signal, μ1(m)≠μ2(m)\mu_{1}^{(m)}\neq\mu_{2}^{(m)}, and the null hypothesis of a constant background rate, μ1(0)=μ2(0)\mu_{1}^{(0)}=\mu_{2}^{(0)}, where μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2} are the predicted numbers of events in two bins of equal integration time. They can be expressed in terms of the expected signal and background rates (μs\mu_{s} and μb\mu_{b}, respectively) for each hypothesis:

μ1(m)=μs​(1+f2)+\displaystyle\mu_{1}^{(m)}=\mu_{s}(1+f_{2})+ μb,μ2(m)=μs​(1−f2)+μb,\displaystyle\mu_{b},\qquad\mu_{2}^{(m)}=\mu_{s}(1-f_{2})+\mu_{b},
μ1(0)=μ2(0)=μb0,\displaystyle\mu_{1}^{(0)}=\mu_{2}^{(0)}=\mu_{b}^{0}, (32)

where f2f_{2} is the integrated modulation fraction defined in Eq. (18), and the significance of a measurement of the number of events in each bin N1N_{1} and N2N_{2} can be assessed using Eq. (31). In terms of R⁡(t)R(t) from Eq. (15), μs\mu_{s} is

μs=12​Texp​⟨R⟩,\displaystyle\mu_{s}=\frac{1}{2}T_{\text{exp}}\langle R\rangle, (33)

where ⟨R⟩\langle R\rangle is R⁡(t)R(t) averaged over one sidereal day, and TexpT_{\text{exp}} is the total exposure time.

If the background rate were well understood, the total number of events (Ntot=N1+N2N_{\text{tot}}=N_{1}+N_{2}) could be compared to the prediction from the null hypothesis, Ntot(0)=2​μb0=μtotN_{\rm tot}^{(0)}=2\mu_{b}^{0}=\mu_{\rm tot} as a way to discover or exclude particular DM models. Even without knowledge of the background, a small value for NtotN_{\text{tot}} can still be used to rule out those models which predict significantly more events than the measured NtotN_{\text{tot}}, but a larger NtotN_{\text{tot}} cannot be construed as a detection of DM without a better understanding of the background. However, the existence of a modulating signal provides an additional statistical handle on both discovery and exclusion.

Assuming that the background rate is unmodelled, a measurement of NtotN_{\text{tot}} supplies the best-fit values for μb(0)\mu_{b}^{(0)} and μb(m)\mu_{b}^{(m)} in the null and modulating hypotheses, through

μb(0)\displaystyle\mu_{b}^{(0)} =12​Ntot.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}N_{\text{tot}}. μs+μb(m)\displaystyle\mu_{s}+\mu_{b}^{(m)} =12​Ntot.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}N_{\text{tot}}. (34)

All of the information about the signal, μs\mu_{s}, is extracted from the measured value of Δ​N=N+−N−\Delta N=N_{+}-N_{-}, which has expected value

⟨Δ​N⟩=2​f2​(mχ,σ¯e)​μs​(mχ,σ¯e),\displaystyle\langle\Delta N\rangle=2f_{2}(m_{\chi},\overline{\sigma}_{e})\,\mu_{s}(m_{\chi},\overline{\sigma}_{e}), (35)

and we have explicitly specified that both the modulation fraction ff and the signal strength parameter μs\mu_{s} depend on the DM mass mχm_{\chi} and cross section σ¯e\overline{\sigma}_{e}.

In assessing the capabilities of a directional detection experiment in the presence of daily modulation, we ask two questions: which DM models predict modulation signals that are large enough to be detected by the experiment? And, if the experiment measures a null result, which DM models are ruled out? The first question, which determines the discovery significance, can be posed in the context of ruling out the null hypothesis, where μΔ(0)=0\mu_{\Delta}^{(0)}=0:

Nσdisc.​(Δ​N)≃|Δ​N|μtot(0)=|Δ​N|Ntot,\displaystyle N_{\sigma}^{\text{disc.}}(\Delta N)\simeq\frac{|\Delta N|}{\sqrt{\mu_{\rm tot}^{(0)}}}=\frac{|\Delta N|}{\sqrt{N_{\text{tot}}}}, (36)

in the Gaussian limit Ntot≫3N_{\text{tot}}\gg 3. Models that satisfy Nσdisc.​(⟨Δ​N⟩)>3N_{\sigma}^{\text{disc.}}(\langle\Delta N\rangle)>3 or Nσdisc.​(⟨Δ​N⟩)>5N_{\sigma}^{\text{disc.}}(\langle\Delta N\rangle)>5 for this central value, for example, are likely to generate a modulation signal strong enough to claim a detection at the 3​σ3\sigma or 5​σ5\sigma level, respectively. The “Discovery” regions in Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 show Nσdisc.​(2​f2​μs)≥3N_{\sigma}^{\text{disc.}}(2f_{2}\mu_{s})\geq 3 using this central value.

To set exclusion limits, we ask which models are ruled out by a null result, Δ​N≈0\Delta N\approx 0. In this case, we use μΔ(m)=2​f2​μs\mu_{\Delta}^{(m)}=2f_{2}\mu_{s} in Eq. (31):

Nσexcl.​(Δ​N)≃|Δ​N−μΔ(m)|2​(μs+μb(m))=|Δ​N−2​f2​μs|Ntot.\displaystyle N_{\sigma}^{\text{excl.}}(\Delta N)\simeq\frac{|\Delta N-\mu_{\Delta}^{(m)}|}{\sqrt{2(\mu_{s}+\mu_{b}^{(m)})}}=\frac{|\Delta N-2f_{2}\mu_{s}|}{\sqrt{N_{\text{tot}}}}. (37)

The exclusion curves of Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 show the models that would be excluded at the 90% confidence level from a null result Δ​N=0\Delta N=0, using Nσexcl.​(0)>1.65N_{\sigma}^{\text{excl.}}(0)>1.65.

In both examples above, we have taken Δ​N\Delta N to be equal to its expectation value under either the modulating hypothesis (Δ​N=2​μs​f2\Delta N=2\mu_{s}f_{2}) or the null hypothesis (Δ​N=0\Delta N=0), which has allowed us to quantify the significance of a measurement without reference to the log-likelihood ratio: both discovery and exclusion limits are given by

Nσ=2​f2​μsNtot.N_{\sigma}=\frac{2f_{2}\mu_{s}}{\sqrt{N_{\rm tot}}}. (38)

This is simply because the “pp value”, λ\lambda, is equal to 11 at the central value of the double sided distribution Eq. (27), and so the likelihood ratio is trivial. Because μs\mu_{s} is the expected counts per half of a day, we see that 2​μs2\mu_{s} is the exposure times the rate expected in Eq. (15). Thus, Eq. (38) exactly recovers Eq. (19).

To assess a measurement away from the central value with more generality, it is better to use the log-likelihood LL defined exactly in Eq. (27) for each hypothesis. For small λ\lambda, the Nσ​(λ)N_{\sigma}(\lambda) defined in Eq. (31) is approximated by

Nσ​(L)≈(L+ln⁡2π​L+ln⁡π2L+𝒪⁡(1/L2))1/2.\displaystyle N_{\sigma}(L)\approx\left(L+\ln\frac{2}{\pi L}+\frac{\ln\frac{\pi}{2}}{L}+\mathcal{O}(1/L^{2})\right)^{1/2}. (39)

For Nσ≫1N_{\sigma}\gg 1, Eq. (39) can be inverted to give an expression for LL in terms of NσN_{\sigma} and expanded as a series in Nσ−2N_{\sigma}^{-2},

L≃Nσ2+ln⁡(Nσ2​π2)−ln⁡(1−1Nσ2+…).\displaystyle L\simeq N_{\sigma}^{2}+\ln\left(\frac{N_{\sigma}^{2}\pi}{2}\right)-\ln\left(1-\frac{1}{N_{\sigma}^{2}}+\ldots\right). (40)

This expression is particularly useful in the Gaussian limit, where NσN_{\sigma} is given by Eq. (31). To leading order in large NσN_{\sigma},

Δ​L​(Δ​N)≈(Δ​N−2​f2​μs)2Ntot−(Δ​N)2Ntot,\displaystyle\Delta L(\Delta N)\approx\frac{(\Delta N-2f_{2}\mu_{s})^{2}}{N_{\text{tot}}}-\frac{(\Delta N)^{2}}{N_{\text{tot}}}, (41)

where the test statistic Δ​L\Delta L compares a specific modulation model with f2​(mχ,σe)​μs​(mχ,σe)f_{2}(m_{\chi},\sigma_{e})\mu_{s}(m_{\chi},\sigma_{e}) to the null hypothesis, μb(0)=12​Ntot\mu_{b}^{(0)}=\frac{1}{2}N_{\text{tot}}. At the central values of the two distributions, Δ​N=2​f2​μs\Delta N=2f_{2}\mu_{s} and Δ​N=0\Delta N=0, the test statistic takes values of ΔL=∓4f22μs2/Ntot\Delta L=\mp 4f_{2}^{2}\mu_{s}^{2}/N_{\text{tot}}, respectively, and we recover exactly Eq. (38).

For other values of Δ​N\Delta N, still in the Gaussian limit (μs≫3\mu_{s}\gg 3), the significance is found from the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the χ22\chi^{2}_{2} distribution,

CDF⁡(Δ​L)≈1−γ⁡(1,12​Δ​L),\displaystyle{\rm CDF}(\Delta L)\approx 1-\gamma\left(1,\frac{1}{2}\Delta L\right), (42)

where γ\gamma is the lower incomplete Euler gamma function, and where k=1k=1 for the simple two-bin analysis. Generalizing to kk statistically independent pairs of bins, the combined test statistic

Δ​L=∑i=1kΔ​Li\displaystyle\Delta L=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\Delta L_{i} (43)

satisfies a χ2\chi^{2} distribution with 2​k2k degrees of freedom, and its CDF is given by

p≈1−γ⁡(k,12​Δ​L)Γ⁡(k).\displaystyle p\approx 1-\frac{\gamma\left(k,\frac{1}{2}\Delta L\right)}{\Gamma(k)}. (44)

In the limit of very few events, μs≲3\mu_{s}\lesssim 3, the CDF should be evaluated using the Skellam distribution instead, as it ceases to be approximately Gaussian for μ1,2<1\mu_{1,2}<1. However, as it is not possible to resolve an O⁡(10%)O(10\%) modulation fraction with so few events, in this limit a more powerful constraint will come from using Poisson statistics on the total number of events.

B.2 Alternate Derivation with Poisson Statistics

The negative log-likelihood for a Poisson process is

L≡−2​ln⁡λ=2​∑k=1Nbins[νk​(𝜽)−nk+nk​ln⁡(nk/νk​(𝜽))],L\equiv-2\ln\lambda=2\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\rm bins}}\left[\nu_{k}(\bm{\theta})-n_{k}+n_{k}\ln(n_{k}/\nu_{k}(\bm{\theta}))\right], (45)

where νk\nu_{k} is the expected number of events in a bin kk, nkn_{k} is the observed number in that bin, and 𝜽\bm{\theta} are NθN_{\theta} parameters that determine νk\nu_{k}. The statistic LL follows a χ2\chi^{2} distribution of Nbins−NθN_{\rm bins}-N_{\theta} degrees of freedom [99].

If we want to compare the hypothesis of a modulating signal versus the null hypothesis of a nonmodulating signal, we simply take the difference of their log-likelihoods. Since the total number of events in a day is fixed in the two scenarios, and only their distribution throughout the day is varying, we have

ΔL=−2∑k=1Nbinsnkln[νkm​(𝜽m)νk0​(𝜽0)],\Delta L=-2\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\rm bins}}n_{k}\ln\left[\frac{\nu_{k}^{m}(\bm{\theta}^{m})}{\nu_{k}^{0}(\bm{\theta}^{0})}\right], (46)

where νkm\nu_{k}^{m} is the number of expected events assuming a modulating signal and νk0\nu_{k}^{0} is the number of events assuming a constant rate over the course of a day, and we have chosen the sign such that Δ​L<0\Delta L<0 means that modulation is preferred. The distribution of values of |Δ​L||\Delta L| follows a χ2\chi^{2} distribution with the number of degrees of freedom set by the difference between the number of parameters 𝜽m\bm{\theta}^{m} and the number of parameters 𝜽0\bm{\theta}^{0}. Eq. (46) is an exact expression for the improvement in fit when allowing a modulating signal instead of a constant signal, appropriate for whichever event binning is most convenient. Because the total number of events is fixed, this is also the difference of the Kullback-Leibler divergences between these two hypotheses with the data.

Eq. (45) and Eq. (46) are appropriate for any choice of data binning, and can even be used for an unbinned analysis. For simplicity, and to provide an alternative derivation of the results in Sec. B.1, we calculate Eq. (46) for the specific choice of two 12-hour bins per day, here labeled by ++ and −-. The rates per bin are ν±m=ν¯s​(1±f2)+νb\nu_{\pm}^{m}=\bar{\nu}^{s}(1\pm f_{2})+\nu^{b} and ν±0=ν¯s+νb\nu_{\pm}^{0}=\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}, where νb\nu^{b} is the expected background rate and ν¯s\bar{\nu}^{s} is the average expected signal rate per bin.

Let us assume first that the true signal is not modulating: the number of observed counts in each bin in a given day is expected to be equal, such that ⟨nk+⟩=⟨nk−⟩=ν¯s+νb\langle n_{k+}\rangle=\langle n_{k-}\rangle=\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}. In this case, we have

Δ​L\displaystyle\Delta L =−2∑d=1Ndays∑±(ν¯s+νb)ln(1±f2​ν¯sν¯s+νb)\displaystyle=-2\sum_{d=1}^{N_{\rm days}}\sum_{\pm}(\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b})\ln\left(1\pm\frac{f_{2}\bar{\nu}^{s}}{\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}}\right)
=−2∑d=1Ndays(ν¯s+νb)ln[1−(f2​ν¯sν¯s+νb)2]\displaystyle=-2\sum_{d=1}^{N_{\rm days}}(\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b})\ln\left[1-\left(\frac{f_{2}\bar{\nu}^{s}}{\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}}\right)^{2}\right]
≃2​∑d=1Ndaysf22​(ν¯s)2ν¯s+νb,\displaystyle\simeq 2\sum_{d=1}^{N_{\rm days}}\frac{f_{2}^{2}(\bar{\nu}^{s})^{2}}{\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}}, (47)

where in the second step we take the limit f2​ν¯s/(ν¯s+νb)≪1f_{2}\bar{\nu}^{s}/(\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b})\ll 1. We now define Ntot=∑d2​(ν¯s+νb)=2​Ndays​(ν¯s+νb)N_{\rm tot}=\sum_{d}2(\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b})=2N_{\rm days}(\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}) to be the total number of events observed and, to make contact with the preceding section, we define μs=∑dν¯s=Ndays​ν¯s\mu_{s}=\sum_{d}\bar{\nu}^{s}=N_{\rm days}\bar{\nu}^{s} to be half of the total number of signal events expected to be observed over the entire experimental exposure. This gives

Δ​L≃(2​f2​μs)2Ntot\Delta L\simeq\frac{(2f_{2}\mu_{s})^{2}}{N_{\rm tot}} (48)

The observed significance of a signal is therefore χ2=(2​f2​μs)2/Ntot\chi^{2}=(2f_{2}\mu_{s})^{2}/N_{\rm tot}. Conversely, a limit at NσN_{\sigma} significance on a modulating signal is possible when Ntotexcl.≃(2​f2​μs/Nσ)2N_{\rm tot}^{\rm excl.}\simeq(2f_{2}\mu_{s}/N_{\sigma})^{2}. As in the preceding section of this Appendix, because μs\mu_{s} is the expected counts per half of a day, the factor 2​μs2\mu_{s} is the exposure times the rate expected in Eq. (15). Thus, Eq. (48) exactly recovers Eq. (19).

Assuming on the other hand that the signal is modulating, the number of observed counts is no longer expected to be the same in the two bins in a given day. Instead, the counts will be related by ⟨nk±⟩=ν¯s​(1±f2)+νb\langle n_{k\pm}\rangle=\bar{\nu}^{s}(1\pm f_{2})+\nu^{b}. In this case, we have

Δ​L\displaystyle\Delta L =−2∑d=1Ndays∑±[ν¯s(1±f2)+νb]ln(1±f2​ν¯sν¯s+νb)\displaystyle=-2\sum_{d=1}^{N_{\rm days}}\sum_{\pm}[\bar{\nu}^{s}(1\pm f_{2})+\nu^{b}]\ln\left(1\pm\frac{f_{2}\bar{\nu}^{s}}{\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}}\right)
≃−2∑d=1Ndays∑±[ν¯s+νb±f2ν¯s][±f2​ν¯sν¯s+νb−12(f2​ν¯sν¯s+νb)2]\displaystyle\simeq-2\sum_{d=1}^{N_{\rm days}}\sum_{\pm}[\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}\pm f_{2}\bar{\nu}^{s}]\left[\pm\frac{f_{2}\bar{\nu}^{s}}{\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}}-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{f_{2}\bar{\nu}^{s}}{\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}}\right)^{2}\right]
≃−2∑d=1Ndaysf22​(ν¯s)2ν¯s+νb,\displaystyle\simeq-2\sum_{d=1}^{N_{\rm days}}\frac{f_{2}^{2}(\bar{\nu}^{s})^{2}}{\bar{\nu}^{s}+\nu^{b}}, (49)

where the relative sign between Eq. (47) and Eq. (49) is reflective of the choice we made that Δ​L<0\Delta L<0 means that a modulating signal is preferred. The magnitude of the significance is exactly the same as in the prior case, differing only in that the interpretation in this scenario is as discovery of a signal.
